rw: A return policy sets clear rules on time limits, condition and refund type, which protects both the store and the customer and builds trust in the business.

ww.To discourage all returns so sales stay: A return policy is meant to be fair and clear, not to block all returns; discouraging every return would drive customers away and hurt long-term sales.
ww.To raise prices on all returned goods: Return policies do not set prices; raising prices on returned goods is not their function, and prices are decided separately through pricing strategy.
ww.To hide product defects from the buyers: A return policy does not exist to conceal defects; hiding problems is deceptive and illegal, while a policy actually gives buyers a remedy for faulty goods.

rw: Purchasing power is the quantity of goods and services a unit of money can buy; it falls when inflation raises prices and rises when prices drop.

ww.The profit of a business each year: Profit is what a business earns after costs; it measures business performance and has nothing to do with how much goods a consumer's money can buy.
ww.The number of stores in a country each y: The number of stores in a country describes market size or retail presence, not the value of money, so it is unrelated to purchasing power.
ww.The tax on income paid by a worker: Income tax is a government charge on earnings; it can reduce take-home pay, but it is not the definition of purchasing power.

rw: License renewal lets the government confirm the business still meets legal requirements such as safety, tax and zoning rules, so it may keep operating lawfully.

ww.To hire workers for the business and all: Renewing a license has nothing to do with hiring; hiring workers is a human resources activity and is not what a license renewal accomplishes.
ww.To raise prices on the goods that the bu: License renewal is a regulatory step and has no effect on pricing; prices are set by the business based on costs, demand and competition.
ww.To advertise the business to the public: Advertising is a marketing activity done through media; a license renewal is a legal filing and does not promote the business to the public.

rw: A nondisclosure clause binds employees to protect trade secrets, client lists and other confidential information, which guards the firm's competitive advantage even after they leave.

ww.To limit an employee's future pay raises: Pay raises are handled by compensation policy and performance reviews; a nondisclosure clause deals with confidentiality and does not limit an employee's future pay.
ww.To prevent employees from taking vacatio: Vacation time is set by company leave policy and labor agreements; a nondisclosure clause concerns secrecy and has no power to prevent taking vacation.
ww.To give workers ownership of the company: Ownership is gained through stock or equity plans, not a nondisclosure clause, which only restricts sharing information and gives employees no ownership stake.

rw: Franchise agreements require franchisees to follow the franchisor's standards, so changing the recipe without approval breaches the contract and can lead to penalties or termination.

ww.A zoning approval by the city: A zoning approval is a city land-use permission; it is not a contract problem and has nothing to do with changing a recipe without approval.
ww.A trademark expiry ending its rights: A trademark expiring is an intellectual property matter caused by failing to renew; altering a recipe does not by itself end the franchisor's trademark rights.
ww.A tax refund from the city office: A tax refund from the city is a government payment on overpaid taxes and has no link to a franchisee breaking recipe rules in the contract.

rw: A strong opening grabs attention and states the purpose, which gets the audience interested and gives them a clear picture of what to expect from the talk.

ww.Skip the introduction and just start: Skipping the introduction leaves the audience unsure of the topic and purpose, so they have no context and may lose interest early in the presentation.
ww.Read the whole script aloud to them: Reading the whole script aloud is dull and breaks eye contact; good presenters speak naturally using notes, and this is not a good way to open.
ww.Apologize for being nervous at first: Apologizing for nerves draws attention to weakness and lowers credibility; confident presenters begin with a hook or purpose rather than excuses.

rw: Identifying the main concerns and answering each calmly shows the customer they were heard, reduces the emotion and moves toward a solution, which is good communication practice.

ww.Ignore the email and do not reply to the: Ignoring a customer email leaves the concern unresolved and damages the relationship, so staying silent is poor service and may lose the customer for good.
ww.Reply with one word and nothing more at: A one-word reply shows no effort to understand the concerns and would likely upset an already emotional customer even more, so it fails basic service standards.
ww.Forward it to the entire staff to show h: Forwarding a customer's upset email to all staff is unprofessional, spreads private matters unnecessarily and does nothing to address the customer's actual concerns.

rw: A service guarantee promises to correct the problem or refund the customer if service falls short, which builds trust and lowers the buyer's perceived risk.

ww.A fee for using the service each time it: A guarantee is a promise, not a usage charge; a fee paid for each use of the service is a price and is not what a guarantee means.
ww.A warning that service will be late, so: A warning of delays is a notice and not a guarantee; a guarantee commits the firm to making things right, not to expecting late service.
ww.A list of employees who provide the serv: A staff roster names who performs the work but makes no promise about results, so it is not a service guarantee.

rw: Posting answers on signs or the website resolves the common question in advance, saving staff time and customers effort while improving the shopping experience.

ww.Raise prices on all the items sold: Raising prices does not answer customers' repeated question and may even drive away buyers, so it fails to solve the real information gap.
ww.Hide the information from the customers: Hiding information leaves the question unanswered and frustrates customers, which hurts trust and increases the number of people asking staff directly.
ww.Tell customers to stop asking questions: Telling customers to stop asking is rude and drives them away; questions signal an information gap the store should fix instead of silencing.

rw: A price floor is a legal minimum price set above the market price, like a minimum wage, and it can cause surpluses when set above equilibrium.

ww.The lowest shop price: The lowest price a shop charges is just a business pricing decision; a price floor is a government-imposed legal limit, not a store's lowest price.
ww.A tax placed on goods: A tax is a government charge added to a good; a price floor is a legal limit on how low a price may go, not a tax.
ww.A legal maximum price: A legal maximum price is a price ceiling, such as rent control, which is the opposite of a price floor, which sets a minimum.

rw: When the minimum wage exceeds equilibrium, firms hire fewer workers or cut hours because labor costs more, so some workers may lose hours or jobs.

ww.A shortage of workers in the field: A wage set above equilibrium attracts more job seekers while firms demand fewer workers, producing a surplus of labor rather than a shortage of workers.
ww.Lower prices everywhere for all goods: A minimum wage affects labor costs for certain jobs and does not lower prices everywhere; if anything, higher labor costs may push some prices up.
ww.No effect at all on workers or firms: A binding wage floor changes pay and hiring decisions, so it has effects on both workers and firms; claiming no effect ignores basic labor market economics.

rw: Thanking the person and sharing credit with those who helped shows gratitude and humility, and it strengthens teamwork and relationships, which is the mark of emotional intelligence.

ww.Ignore the comment and say nothing to th: Ignoring praise comes across as cold or rude and misses a chance to build goodwill with the person who took the time to give it.
ww.Take all the credit for the work done by: Taking all the credit ignores the contributions of teammates, harms trust and morale, and shows poor emotional intelligence and a lack of humility.
ww.Brag about it to everyone in the office: Bragging to everyone in the office comes across as arrogant, damages relationships and does not show emotional intelligence, which values humility and respect for others.

rw: A pitch is a short, focused presentation used to persuade investors, partners or customers to back an idea, so it must be clear, convincing and brief.

ww.A legal contract between a firm and a bu: A legal contract between a firm and a buyer is a sales agreement; it records terms of a deal and is not what an entrepreneur's pitch is.
ww.A product recall issued by a firm for an: A product recall is a corrective action for unsafe goods; it is unrelated to presenting a business idea to investors or partners.
ww.A tax form that a small business must fi: A tax form is a government filing a business completes each year, and it has nothing to do with presenting a business idea to supporters.

rw: Adapting marketing to the target market means using messages and channels that suit busy parents, such as social media, convenience and time-saving benefits.

ww.Target teenagers only, with ads for scho: Targeting only teenagers ignores her actual customer base of parents; marketing works best when the message matches who really buys the product.
ww.Use messages for retirees, who have more: Retirees are not her main customers, and having more savings does not make them the right audience, so messages aimed at them would miss her market.
ww.Avoid all advertising to parents and fam: Avoiding advertising to parents would cut her off from her best customers; she should reach existing buyers rather than ignore them in her marketing.

rw: Net profit margin equals net income divided by sales, shown as a percent; for example, $10,000 net income on $100,000 in sales is a 10 percent margin.

ww.Sales divided by the units: Sales divided by units sold gives average selling price per unit, not a margin, because it does not include any costs or profit measure.
ww.Assets divided by liabilities: Assets divided by liabilities is a solvency measure that compares what a firm owns to what it owes; it is not a profit margin.
ww.Expenses divided by assets: Expenses divided by assets is not a standard profitability ratio; net profit margin compares net income to sales, not expenses to assets.

rw: Net income = $90,000 sales - $45,000 cost of goods sold - $20,000 other expenses = $25,000, which is what remains after all costs.

ww.$45,000: $45,000 is the cost of goods sold alone, or gross profit; it ignores the $20,000 of other expenses that must still be subtracted to find net income.
ww.$155,000: $155,000 results from adding the costs to sales ($90,000 + $45,000 + $20,000); costs must be subtracted from sales, not added to them.
ww.$65,000: $65,000 comes from subtracting only the $25,000 of costs combined wrongly, instead of subtracting both $45,000 and $20,000 from $90,000, which correctly leaves $25,000.

rw: A mentorship program pairs experienced employees with newer ones so that they can pass on skills, advice and company knowledge, which builds careers and improves retention.

ww.A schedule of vacations for the employee: A vacation schedule is a leave calendar for staff; it does not match experienced and newer employees, so it is not a mentorship program.
ww.A list of customers and the goods that t: A list of customers and their purchases is a sales or customer record, which has nothing to do with developing employees through guidance.
ww.A pay chart showing wages for each job g: A pay chart showing wages by job grade is a compensation structure; it sets pay levels rather than providing mentoring support to employees.

rw: A data privacy policy tells customers and staff how the company collects, uses, stores and protects personal data, helping it meet laws and build trust.

ww.A sales forecast made for the next year: A sales forecast predicts future revenue and is a planning tool; it says nothing about how the company handles customer data.
ww.A list of employees and their jobs in th: A list of employees and their jobs is an organization chart or directory, which describes roles and does not explain data handling practices.
ww.A product warranty that comes with goods: A product warranty promises repair or replacement of goods; it covers product defects and has nothing to do with how data is handled.

rw: A sales report from the database quickly shows units sold by product, so the manager can identify last quarter's best seller accurately and efficiently.

ww.Guessing from memory alone now: Guessing from memory is unreliable and can be wrong, so it is not an efficient or accurate way to identify the best seller.
ww.Asking every customer by phone: Phoning every customer is extremely slow and costly, and customers' recollections would be less reliable than the sales data the firm already holds.
ww.Counting receipts by hand only: Counting receipts by hand takes far too long and invites errors when a database report can give the answer in seconds.

rw: A call to action tells the audience what to do next, such as "buy now" or "call today", and it turns interest into a response.

ww.The company's address only, shown in sma: A company address in small print may help contact, but it does not urge the audience to take a specific step, so it is not a call to action.
ww.A list of product ingredients printed on: A list of ingredients is product information printed on the package; it informs buyers but does not tell them what action to take next.
ww.A legal warning printed at the bottom of: A legal warning is a disclosure required for safety or compliance; it does not prompt the audience to take a buying step.

rw: Surveying a sample of people about whether they recognize the brand directly measures awareness, which is the share of the market that knows the brand.

ww.Count its employees and the hours that e: Counting employees and their hours measures staffing and labor, which says nothing about whether the public recognizes the brand.
ww.Review its rent costs for the last three: Rent costs are an operating expense and reveal nothing about how many people recognize the brand, so they are not a measure of awareness.
ww.Check its tax records to see what it pai: Tax records show what the company paid in taxes, which is a financial matter and not a direct measure of public brand awareness.

rw: Inventory turnover shows how many times a firm sells and replaces its inventory in a period, calculated as cost of goods sold divided by average inventory.

ww.The number of employees working at the f: The number of employees working each day is a staffing measure; inventory turnover relates to goods sold and replaced, not to workforce size.
ww.The size of the warehouse where all good: Warehouse size describes storage capacity and is not a ratio of sales activity; turnover measures how fast stock moves, not how much space it uses.
ww.The price of goods sold by the firm to i: The price of goods sold to buyers is the selling price; turnover is a ratio of how quickly inventory sells, not a price.

rw: Turnover of 4 instead of 8 means inventory is being sold and replaced half as often, so stock is selling more slowly, tying up cash and risking obsolescence.

ww.Sales are totally unaffected: Turnover falling from 8 to 4 shows a major change in how fast stock moves, so sales are clearly affected rather than unchanged.
ww.The store has no inventory: A store with no inventory would have no turnover to calculate at all, yet the ratio is still 4, so stock exists and is selling.
ww.Stock is selling twice as fast: Stock selling twice as fast would raise turnover from 8 to 16, not lower it from 8 to 4, which is the opposite direction.

rw: A career goal gives direction to education and work choices, such as courses, training and jobs, so efforts stay focused on the career you want.

ww.To avoid work and any form of effort at: A career goal is meant to drive effort and purpose, not to avoid work, so this option reverses its actual purpose.
ww.To prevent learning new skills in a care: Career goals encourage learning new skills to reach the goal; they do not prevent skill growth, which is needed for advancement.
ww.To limit your options so you stay in one: Goals expand and guide options, they do not trap you in one job; people often change jobs and paths while working toward them.

rw: Listening, asking clarifying questions and making an improvement plan shows maturity and a growth mindset, and it helps you correct the issue and strengthen trust with your supervisor.

ww.Ignore the feedback and carry on exactly: Ignoring feedback shows poor professionalism and wastes a chance to improve; supervisors expect employees to act on constructive criticism.
ww.Argue and blame others for the issues th: Arguing and blaming others avoids responsibility and damages the working relationship, which makes it an unprofessional response to criticism.
ww.Quit immediately and walk out of the off: Quitting in anger is an immature reaction that harms your reputation and career and fixes none of the problems raised.

rw: Stakeholder analysis identifies the groups affected by a decision, such as employees, customers and investors, and weighs their interests and influence to plan communication and reduce conflict.

ww.Designing a logo for the brand that the: Logo design is a branding task handled by designers; stakeholder analysis does not deal with artwork or brand visuals at all.
ww.Setting product prices for the goods tha: Product pricing relies on cost, demand and competition analysis, not on stakeholder analysis, which examines who is affected by decisions.
ww.Counting inventory in the warehouse at t: Counting inventory is an operations and accounting task done through stock counts, and it is unrelated to analyzing stakeholders.

rw: Differentiation means offering unique features, quality or service that rivals lack, which gives customers a reason to choose the new entrant despite strong local competition.

ww.Charge the same price with no real diffe: Charging the same price with no difference gives buyers no reason to switch from established local competitors, so it does not set the firm apart.
ww.Copy competitors exactly, down to their: Copying competitors exactly, including prices, makes the company look identical and offers customers no reason to choose the newcomer over local firms.
ww.Hide the product from local customers an: Hiding the product from local customers would produce no sales at all, so it cannot be a strategy to compete in the market.

rw: Regulatory compliance means obeying the laws and regulations that apply to the business, such as safety, labor, tax and consumer protection rules, to avoid penalties.

ww.Setting its own industry standards for r: Rival firms follow their own industry practices; setting standards for them is not compliance, which is about the business obeying existing rules.
ww.Avoiding all government inspections of i: Compliance does not avoid inspections; inspectors check that a firm obeys rules, and avoiding them would suggest the firm is hiding violations.
ww.Choosing the cheapest legal option even: Picking the cheapest option that harms buyers breaks consumer protection duties; compliance requires following the law, even when a cheaper path exists.

rw: Food storage temperatures are governed by health and safety regulations, which exist to prevent foodborne illness, so unsafe temperatures violate this type of compliance.

ww.Advertising regulations only: Advertising regulations cover truthful claims in promotions and do not govern food storage temperatures, so this is the wrong type of compliance.
ww.Tax regulations on income: Tax regulations deal with reporting and paying taxes on income, and storing food too warm is not a tax issue.
ww.Labor classification rules: Labor classification rules decide whether workers are employees or contractors; they do not address food safety or storage temperature.

rw: OSHA, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, sets and enforces workplace safety and health standards, inspects employers and can issue fines for violations.

ww.The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency: The EPA protects the environment by regulating pollution and chemicals; it does not set workplace safety standards for employees.
ww.Securities and Exchange Commission, for: The SEC regulates securities markets and investor disclosure, and it has no authority over workplace safety rules.
The FTC enforces consumer protection and competition law, such as false advertising; it does not oversee safety in the workplace.

rw: Wage and hour laws such as the FLSA require records, which let the employer prove compliance and defend against claims during an audit or dispute.

ww.To meet the legal requirements for adver: Advertising law concerns truthful claims in promotions; employee hour and pay records are kept under labor law and are not an advertising requirement.
ww.To help set next year's prices for all o: Prices are set by costs, demand and competition; payroll records are kept for legal reasons and are not mainly used for pricing products.
ww.To qualify for a discount on shipping an: Shipping discounts depend on carrier agreements and shipping volume, and payroll records have no role in getting a freight discount.

rw: A compliance officer makes sure company policies and operations follow applicable laws and regulations, trains staff and monitors for violations to reduce legal risk.

ww.Setting the monthly sales targets for ea: Setting monthly sales targets belongs to sales management, not to the compliance officer, whose role is legal and regulatory oversight.
ww.Recruiting and hiring new employees for: Recruiting and hiring are human resources duties; a compliance officer checks that hiring follows laws but does not recruit workers.
ww.Designing the packaging that products ar: Package design is a marketing and product task; the compliance officer would only check that packaging meets legal labeling rules.

rw: Noncompliance can lead to fines, lawsuits, lost licenses and damage to reputation, which is why firms invest in compliance programs.

ww.Lower taxes for the firm too: Failing to follow regulations does not lower taxes; if anything, violations may add back taxes, interest and penalties for the firm.
ww.Higher supplier discounts too: Suppliers do not reward a firm for breaking rules, and violations can damage relationships, so higher supplier discounts are not a result.
ww.Automatic license renewals: Regulators may refuse to renew or may even revoke licenses for violations, so automatic renewals are not a likely result of noncompliance.

rw: A project is temporary, with a defined start and finish and a specific result, unlike everyday operations, which are ongoing and repetitive.

ww.It repeats forever with the same tasks: Repeating the same tasks forever describes ongoing operations; a project is a temporary effort that ends, so this option describes operations.
ww.It has no specific goal at any time: Every project is created to achieve a specific goal; a project with no goal would have nothing to deliver or measure.
ww.It needs no resources of any kind: Projects always need resources such as people, money, time and materials, so a project needing none of them could not be carried out.

rw: A chart of tasks, owners and due dates, like a Gantt chart or task tracker, schedules the work and tracks progress against deadlines.

ww.Recruiting new staff for the team: Recruiting staff is a human resources process and does not rely on a chart listing tasks, owners and due dates.
ww.Forecasting product demand for next year: Demand forecasting uses sales history and market data rather than a chart of tasks, owners and deadlines, so this is not its use.
ww.Calculating payroll taxes owed each mont: Payroll taxes are computed from wages and tax rates, not from a task chart, which has no pay data in it.

rw: Scope defines the work included in the project and what is excluded, which prevents scope creep and keeps the team focused on agreed deliverables.

ww.The legal structure of the company and a: The legal structure and ownership of a company is a business formation matter and does not define what a project covers.
ww.The pay of the team members who work on: Team pay belongs to the budget and compensation, not to scope; scope defines the work and deliverables.
ww.The number of customers served after the: Customers served after launch is a result or outcome measure and does not define the work covered by the project.

rw: The first step is to assess the effect on time, cost and scope, then agree the change formally with the client, which is proper change control.

ww.Refuse all changes regardless of how val: Refusing all changes ignores valuable requests and harms the client relationship; project managers should evaluate changes instead of rejecting them outright.
ww.Pause the whole project until the client: Pausing the whole project delays the work and wastes resources; the correct response is to review the change request, not stop everything.
ww.Accept every change at once without chec: Accepting changes without checking can blow the budget and schedule, which is scope creep; changes must be evaluated and approved first.

rw: Time and cost are two classic project constraints, along with scope and quality; changing one usually affects the others, often called the triple constraint.

ww.Price and place: Price and place are two of the four Ps of the marketing mix, not project constraints, which are mostly time, cost and scope.
ww.Color and size: Color and size are product attributes and not classic project constraints, which relate to schedule, budget and scope.
ww.People and brand: People and brand are not among the classic project constraints, which are time, cost and scope or quality.

rw: A risk register lists possible problems, the likelihood and impact of each, and planned responses, so the team can manage threats before they hurt the project.

ww.The salaries and pay rates of all of the: Salaries and pay rates belong in the budget or payroll records, not in a risk register, which tracks potential problems.
ww.The final results and deliverables of th: Final results and deliverables are recorded in the project scope and completion reports, not in the risk register, which tracks possible problems.
ww.Only the contact details of the project': Supplier contact details belong in a stakeholder or contact list; a risk register tracks risks, not contact information.

rw: Knowledge management is the practice of capturing, organizing and sharing what an organization knows so employees can use it, which improves decisions and avoids repeated work.

ww.Hiring new employees to fill vacant posi: Hiring to fill vacancies is a human resources function; it adds staff but does not capture or share what the organization knows.
ww.Setting the prices charged for the compa: Setting product prices is a pricing decision made on costs, demand and competition, so it is not knowledge management.
ww.Auditing a company's financial statement: Auditing financial statements checks accuracy of accounts, which is an accounting task and not about managing organizational knowledge.

rw: Tacit knowledge is gained from experience and is hard to write down, like a veteran technician's instinct for diagnosing faults that is not in any manual.

ww.A written user manual that comes with th: A written user manual is explicit knowledge because it is already documented and can be easily shared with others.
ww.A database containing the details of pas: A database of past orders holds recorded data, which makes it explicit knowledge and not tacit knowledge, which is held in people's minds.
ww.A safety checklist posted on the wall of: A posted safety checklist is written down and shared, so it is explicit knowledge rather than tacit knowledge.

rw: An internal searchable knowledge base stores answers and guides in one place, letting employees find information quickly without interrupting a coworker.

ww.A paper time sheet for hourly staff: A paper time sheet records hours worked for payroll, and it contains no answers to employees' common work questions.
ww.An annual report for the investors: An annual report summarizes company results for investors and does not answer employees' day-to-day how-to questions.
ww.A supplier invoice sent for payment: A supplier invoice is a bill requesting payment and gives no help in answering employees' common questions.

rw: Documenting key processes and pairing the employee with a successor transfers both written and tacit knowledge, so the company keeps it after retirement.

ww.Rely on their old email archive alone to: Relying on an email archive alone captures messages but not judgment and know-how, and it is hard to search, so much knowledge is lost.
ww.Delete their old files to save space on: Deleting the files would destroy valuable knowledge the company might need; saving server space does not justify losing what the senior employee created.
ww.Ask them to keep working without pay aft: Asking a retiree to work without pay is unfair and likely illegal; it does not capture knowledge for the organization.

rw: When employees share knowledge, lessons are not lost, so teams avoid repeating the same mistakes, saving time and money and improving quality.

ww.Larger inventory stocks: Inventory levels are driven by demand and supply planning and are not a benefit of sharing knowledge across a company.
ww.Higher office rent costs: Higher rent costs result from property markets and lease terms and are not a benefit of sharing knowledge.
ww.Longer team meetings daily: Longer meetings are a cost, not a benefit; good knowledge sharing aims to make work more efficient, not to lengthen meetings.

rw: Quality control checks products or services against set standards to find defects before they reach customers, using inspection and testing.

ww.Setting the prices charged for the compa: Setting prices is a pricing function; quality control focuses on checking that products meet standards, not on setting prices.
ww.Advertising the company to attract new c: Advertising attracts customers and is a marketing activity; it is unrelated to inspecting output against standards, which is quality control.
ww.Hiring temporary staff during a busy sal: Hiring temporary staff for busy seasons is a staffing decision and is not part of quality control.

rw: The defect rate measures defective items per number produced, such as per 1,000 units, and helps track quality and spot process problems.

ww.Staff turnover: Staff turnover measures how many employees leave a firm in a period, which has nothing to do with counting defective items.
ww.Stock turnover: Stock turnover measures how often inventory is sold and replaced, so it relates to inventory management rather than defects per 1,000 units.
ww.Return on sales: Return on sales is a profitability ratio of profit to sales, and it does not count defective items.

rw: Continuous improvement means making ongoing small changes that gradually raise quality and efficiency, as seen in practices such as Kaizen and lean methods.

ww.Leaving processes unchanged once they ar: Leaving processes unchanged once approved is the opposite of continuous improvement, which keeps looking for better ways of working.
ww.Replacing the whole business every singl: Replacing the whole business every year would be wasteful and disruptive; continuous improvement is about small, steady refinements rather than total replacement.
ww.Changing only when customers complain lo: Changing only when customers complain is reactive; continuous improvement looks for problems and chances to improve before complaints arise.

rw: A checklist that confirms food temperatures and cleanliness each shift prevents problems before they happen, which is a quality assurance process.

ww.Price skimming strategy: Price skimming is a pricing strategy of starting high on a new product, which is unrelated to a shift checklist for food safety.
ww.Capital budgeting process: Capital budgeting is evaluating large long-term investments, and a food safety checklist is not a capital investment decision.
ww.Market segmentation of buyers: Market segmentation divides buyers into groups with similar traits; a temperature and cleanliness checklist does nothing to separate buyers.

rw: The customer is the ultimate judge of quality because quality is defined by how well a product meets customer needs and expectations.

ww.A supplier: A supplier provides inputs but does not use the finished product the way buyers do, so the supplier is not the final judge of quality.
ww.An accountant: An accountant records and reports financial data, but accountants do not decide whether a product satisfies buyers.
ww.A competitor: A competitor has an interest in winning sales and does not set the standard for what your customers value.

rw: Insurance transfers the financial risk of loss to the insurer in exchange for a premium, which is a classic example of risk transfer.

ww.Increasing the risk: Buying insurance lowers a firm's financial exposure and does not increase the risk, which is the opposite of what insurance does.
ww.Avoiding risk: Avoiding risk means not doing the risky activity at all; buying insurance still allows the activity and moves the cost of loss to the insurer.
ww.Ignoring risk: Ignoring risk means doing nothing about it; paying an insurance premium is an active step to deal with potential loss.

rw: Installing security systems and training staff lowers the chance or size of theft losses, which is risk reduction, also called mitigation.

ww.Avoidance: Avoidance would mean not operating in a way that exposes the shop to theft at all, which is not what installing security does.
ww.Transfer: Transfer shifts the cost of loss to another party, such as an insurer, but security and training prevent theft directly.
ww.Acceptance: Acceptance means taking the risk without action, but this shop is acting to lower the chance of theft.

rw: Speculative risk offers a chance of gain or loss, like investing in a new product, which could earn a profit or lose money.

ww.A warehouse fire that destroys all of a: A warehouse fire only causes loss and has no chance of gain, so it is a pure risk and not a speculative risk.
ww.A car accident involving a company van t: A van accident can only create loss for the company, which makes it a pure risk, not a speculative one.
ww.A flood that damages a company's main of: A flood damaging an office can only cause a loss, so it is a pure risk with no possible profit.

rw: Avoidance eliminates the risk by choosing not to engage in the risky activity, so dropping a product line with serious safety concerns is risk avoidance.

ww.Retention: Retention means accepting the risk and bearing the loss, but this company is stopping the activity altogether, not accepting the risk.
ww.Reduction: Reduction lowers the chance or impact of loss while continuing the activity, but this company stops selling the product line instead.
ww.Transfer: Transfer shifts the risk to another party such as an insurer, but the company here removes the risk by dropping the line.

rw: The first step is to identify possible risks, because a business cannot assess, rank or respond to risks it has not recognized.

ww.Buy insurance for the firm: Buying insurance is a risk response used after risks have been identified and assessed, so it cannot be the first step.
ww.Pay out all the claims: Paying claims occurs after a loss happens and is a late step, far from the planning stage at the start of the process.
ww.Report results publicly: Reporting results comes after risks are identified, treated and monitored, so it is a late step rather than the first.

rw: A ledger is the book of accounts that records and summarizes a business's transactions by account, and its balances feed the financial statements.

ww.A marketing report that tracks the resul: A report tracking ad results is a marketing analysis document and does not record accounts or transactions as a ledger does.
ww.A type of business loan from a local ban: A loan is borrowed money from a lender; a ledger is an accounting record, not a type of financing.
ww.A tax form that a small business files e: A tax form is a government filing; a ledger is an internal accounting record used to prepare many reports, including tax filings.

rw: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's equity is the basic accounting equation, showing that what a firm owns is financed by creditors and owners.

ww.Assets = Liabilities - Owner's equity: Subtracting owner's equity from liabilities is wrong; the equation says assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity, never minus.
ww.Assets + Liabilities = Owner's equity: Adding assets and liabilities to equal equity is wrong, because assets equal liabilities plus equity rather than the other way around.
ww.Revenue = Expenses + Owner's equity: Revenue equals expenses plus equity is not the accounting equation; revenue and expenses are income statement items, not the balance sheet equation.

rw: Accrual accounting records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when cash changes hands, giving a fuller picture of performance.

ww.Cash basis accounting: Cash basis accounting records sales only when cash is received, so recording a sale before payment would not fit this method.
ww.Budget accounting: Budget accounting is not a standard method for recording earned revenue; a budget is a plan of expected income and spending.
ww.Cost accounting: Cost accounting tracks and analyzes production costs for management and does not decide when sales revenue is recorded.

rw: Money owed to a supplier is recorded as accounts payable, a liability, so an unpaid $1,200 invoice increases accounts payable by $1,200.

ww.As an increase in accounts receivable: Accounts receivable is money customers owe the business; an unpaid supplier invoice is money the business owes, so receivables do not rise.
ww.As a decrease in all the expenses: An unpaid supplier invoice does not reduce expenses; the cost may add to expenses or assets while the obligation to pay is recorded.
ww.As a decrease in total liabilities: Owing a supplier raises what the firm owes, so liabilities increase and do not decrease when an invoice is received.

rw: Accounting software, such as QuickBooks, records daily transactions, tracks accounts and produces reports, which is why small businesses commonly use it.

ww.Email client software: Email software is for communication and has no accounting functions such as ledgers or financial statements.
ww.Photo-editing software: Photo-editing software edits images and cannot record or total financial transactions.
ww.Presentation software: Presentation software creates slides for meetings and does not record or organize financial transactions.

rw: Reconciliation compares the business's books to the bank statement to find differences such as errors, fees or missed deposits, so records stay accurate.

ww.To raise their credit score automaticall: Reconciling bank statements does not raise a credit score, which depends on borrowing and payment history reported to credit bureaus.
ww.To earn higher interest from the bank ea: Interest paid by the bank depends on account terms and balance, and reconciling does not change it.
ww.To reduce the taxes they owe to the stat: Taxes are based on taxable income and tax law; reconciling bank statements checks accuracy and does not lower the tax owed.

rw: The accounting cycle starts by analyzing transactions, then journalizing them, then posting to the ledger, in that order.

ww.Post to the ledger, analyze transactions: Posting to the ledger before analyzing and journalizing reverses the order; transactions must be analyzed and recorded in a journal first.
ww.Journalize, close the books, then analyz: Closing the books occurs at the end of the cycle, so journalizing, closing and then analyzing gets the sequence badly wrong.
ww.Close the books, then post to the ledger: Closing the books is a late step, so putting it first and then posting before journalizing reverses the cycle.

rw: Knowledge management is capturing, sharing and using what an organization knows, so employees can make better decisions and avoid repeating work.

ww.Deleting old documents to free up storag: Deleting old documents to save space is data cleanup and does not capture, share or use organizational knowledge.
ww.Keeping information secret from every em: Keeping information secret from all employees defeats knowledge management, whose aim is to make knowledge available to those who need it.
ww.Buying new computers for the whole offic: Buying new computers is a technology purchase and does not itself capture or share the organization's knowledge.

rw: Explicit knowledge can be written down, recorded and shared, such as in manuals, reports and databases, which makes it easy to transfer.

ww.Knowledge people hold in their heads fro: Knowledge people hold in their heads from experience is tacit knowledge, which is hard to write down, not explicit knowledge.
ww.Knowledge that is protected by a legal p: Patents are a legal protection for inventions and do not define what explicit knowledge is, which concerns form rather than legal status.
ww.Knowledge that no one in the company can: If no one can explain knowledge, it cannot be written down, which makes it tacit, the opposite of explicit knowledge.

rw: Tacit knowledge comes from experience and personal insight and is hard to put into words, like the know-how of a skilled craftsperson.

ww.Knowledge shared in a company newsletter: Knowledge in a company newsletter is written and shared, which makes it explicit knowledge rather than tacit knowledge.
ww.Knowledge that is printed on the company: Knowledge on a website is published and easily accessed, so it is explicit rather than tacit.
ww.Knowledge that is stored in a printed ma: Knowledge stored in a printed manual is documented, which makes it explicit knowledge and not tacit knowledge.

rw: Fixing machines by feel with no written steps is tacit knowledge, which comes from experience and is difficult to document or transfer.

ww.Legal knowledge: Legal knowledge refers to laws and regulations, which does not describe a skill learned by feel and never written down.
ww.Public knowledge: Public knowledge is information available to everyone, but a technician's skill by feel is personal and not openly shared.
ww.Explicit knowledge: Explicit knowledge is written down or recorded, but this technician has no written steps, so the knowledge is not explicit.

rw: A knowledge base is a searchable collection of information, such as FAQs and guides, that staff can use to find answers quickly.

ww.A group of experts who work together on: A group of experts working together is a project team and is not a collection of searchable information.
ww.A report that lists a firm's yearly prof: A report of profits and costs is a financial statement and does not serve as a store of searchable knowledge.
ww.A building where a firm stores its produ: A building for storing products is a warehouse, which holds goods and not information.

rw: Documented processes let others follow the same steps and keep knowledge in the company when people leave, which supports consistency and training.

ww.So that competitors can copy the whole b: Documentation is meant to help the company, and sharing plans with competitors would harm its competitive advantage.
ww.So that the firm can avoid following any: Documented processes help firms follow rules consistently, so they do not let a company avoid rules.
ww.So that no employee will ever need any f: Documentation supports training, but it does not remove the need for training; new tasks and updates still require learning.

rw: Documenting key processes and pairing the retiring employee with a successor transfers knowledge before they leave, so the company keeps it.

ww.Wait until the employee leaves, then ask: Waiting until the employee leaves means the knowledge may be forgotten or lost, so asking afterward is too late.
ww.Delete the employee's files on the very: Deleting files on the last day would destroy useful records and knowledge, the opposite of protecting it.
ww.Hire someone who has never seen the work: Hiring someone with no experience in the work does not preserve existing knowledge and would require learning from scratch.

rw: A best practice is a method proven to produce excellent results, so it is shared and used as a standard for others.

ww.A method used only once by one employee: A method used only once by one employee has not been proven or shared, so it is not a best practice.
ww.A method that is required by no one here: A method that no one requires has not been tested or shown to work, so it is not a best practice, which is proven to give excellent results.
ww.A method that is cheapest regardless of: Cheapest regardless of results ignores quality, so it does not describe a best practice, which is judged by results.

rw: An intranet is a private network inside an organization that lets employees share information, documents and tools securely.

ww.A device that stores backup tapes for al: A device that stores backup tapes is a storage system and does not describe a network used inside the organization.
ww.A public website where customers buy the: A public website where customers buy products is an e-commerce site, which is open to the public and not an internal network.
ww.A social network used by teenagers to sh: A social network used by teenagers is a public consumer platform and not a private business network.

rw: A lesson learned is insight from a project's successes and failures that can be applied to improve future projects.

ww.A rule that prevents mistakes in all cas: A rule that prevents mistakes in all cases claims too much; lessons learned are insights, not absolute guarantees against errors.
ww.A class that employees attend every year: A class that renews licenses is formal training and not an insight gained from a project's experience.
ww.A report that lists employees' pay and h: A report on pay and hours is a payroll record and does not capture insights from project experience.

rw: Writing down what went wrong after a failed launch captures lessons learned, so the team can avoid repeating the same mistakes.

ww.Hiding the failure from teams: Hiding the failure prevents learning, so it is the opposite of recording lessons from what went wrong.
ww.Blaming one person for it: Blaming one person does not explain what went wrong and discourages open sharing, so it fails to capture lessons.
ww.Deleting all launch records: Deleting the records destroys the information needed to learn from the failure, so it is the opposite of capturing lessons.

rw: Data is raw facts and figures, such as numbers or names, that have not yet been organized or interpreted.

ww.A plan for reaching goals: A plan for reaching goals is a strategy, which uses information, but it is not raw facts and figures.
ww.Skill gained from work: Skill gained from work is experience or expertise, which is a personal capability and not raw data.
ww.Conclusions drawn from it: Conclusions drawn from data are information or insight, which come after data has been analyzed.

rw: Information is data that has been processed, organized and given meaning so it can support understanding and decisions.

ww.A private opinion not shared with others: A private opinion is a personal view and is not information, which is data organized and given meaning.
ww.Unprocessed numbers in a long list of da: Unprocessed numbers in a long list are raw data, which becomes information only after being organized and interpreted.
ww.A guess about the future with no evidenc: A guess with no evidence is speculation; information is based on organized data, so a guess is not information.

rw: The manager organized the raw sales numbers into a meaningful trend, a 10 percent monthly rise, which is information created from data.

ww.Data from information: Data does not come from information; the process runs the other way, with information created from raw data.
ww.A secret not to be shared: A trend that the manager shares with others is not a secret, and it comes from real numbers.
ww.A guess without any data: The manager used actual sales numbers, so the conclusion about a 10 percent monthly rise is not a guess without data.

rw: Cloud storage keeps files on remote servers online, so they can be reached from many devices and shared with others.

ww.Printing documents at high speed on pape: Printing documents is the job of printers and has nothing to do with online file storage in the cloud.
ww.Making the weather more predictable for: The cloud in cloud storage is a network of servers, not weather, and it has no effect on weather.
ww.Hiding files from every single employee: Cloud storage is meant to make files accessible to authorized users, not to hide them from everyone.

rw: Restricting access protects sensitive information, such as financial and personal data, from theft, leaks and misuse, and helps meet legal duties.

ww.To lower the cost of storage for the fir: Limiting access is about security, not cost, since storage costs do not fall because fewer people can open confidential files.
ww.To make it harder for the owners to find: Limiting access does not make files harder for authorized owners to find; it blocks unauthorized people while allowing proper access.
ww.To keep customers from ever paying the b: Access limits do not stop customers from paying, and they are a security measure, not a billing control.

rw: A community of practice is a group sharing a field or interest who learn from each other by exchanging experience and tips.

ww.A group of suppliers who set prices toge: Suppliers who set prices together would be price fixing, which is illegal and not a community of practice.
ww.A group of rivals who hide information f: Rivals hiding information from each other is the opposite of a community of practice, whose purpose is sharing knowledge.
ww.A group of customers who buy the same pr: Customers who review a product form a customer group, not a community of practice, which is a group of practitioners learning together.

rw: Mentoring means experienced employees guide less experienced ones, passing on skills, advice and company knowledge to help them grow.

ww.Managers firing employees who make mista: Firing employees who make mistakes is punishment and not mentoring, which is meant to guide and develop people.
ww.Employees competing for one promotion ea: Competing for a single promotion is rivalry, while mentoring is a cooperative relationship in which one person helps another grow.
ww.Customers training staff to sell product: Customers training staff to sell is not mentoring, which involves experienced colleagues within the organization guiding newer staff.

rw: Reviewing and updating documents on a regular schedule removes outdated information and keeps knowledge accurate and useful.

ww.Delete any document older than a single: Deleting every document after one day would destroy knowledge, so it does not keep knowledge current, only erase it.
ww.Let each employee keep personal copies o: Personal copies only would scatter knowledge and let copies become outdated, which defeats a shared and current knowledge system.
ww.Never change documents once they are wri: Never changing documents lets them become outdated and wrong, so knowledge is not kept current.

rw: A database stores organized information so it can be searched, updated and shared, making knowledge easy to find and keep accurate.

ww.Printing posters for a store event with: Printing posters is a print and marketing job, which a database does not do, since it stores and retrieves information.
ww.Moving products to customers by truck, v: Moving products by truck, van or train is transportation and logistics, which is not the job of a database.
ww.Keeping the time for employee shifts and: Tracking shift times is a scheduling or payroll function and not the main knowledge management use of a database.

rw: A searchable help center gives customers ready answers to common questions, so fewer ask the support team and workload falls.

ww.A longer list of staff holidays for the: A list of staff holidays gives leave dates and does nothing to answer customers' repeated questions or reduce the support workload.
ww.A bigger parking lot for staff and visit: A bigger parking lot is a facilities matter and has no effect on the volume of questions the support team receives.
ww.A new color for the company's logo and s: A new logo color changes appearance only and does not help answer customers' questions, so the workload would remain.

rw: Intellectual property is creations of the mind, such as inventions, brands and written works, that are legally protected by patents, trademarks and copyrights.

ww.Buildings and land owned by a company an: Buildings and land are physical or tangible assets recorded on the balance sheet, not creations of the mind, so they are not intellectual property.
ww.Furniture used in an office, such as des: Office furniture is a tangible asset that is physically used in the office, which makes it equipment and not intellectual property.
ww.Cash held in a company bank account, on: Cash in a bank account is a financial asset earning interest, and it is not a creation of the mind protected by law.

rw: Trade secret protection, including limited access and confidentiality agreements, keeps a recipe valuable by controlling who can learn it and how it is used.

ww.Sharing it with all competitors so that: Sharing the recipe with competitors would let them copy the product and destroy its value, the opposite of keeping it confidential.
ww.Publishing the recipe on the company web: Publishing the recipe on a website makes it public and ends its secrecy, so it would no longer be a protected secret.
ww.Printing it on every package so that any: Printing the recipe on every package discloses it to everyone, which destroys its secrecy and its competitive value.

rw: An after-action review discusses what happened, why it happened and how to improve next time, turning experience into lessons for future work.

ww.A list of employees who left the project: A list of people who left a project early is a staffing record and does not analyze what happened or how to improve.
ww.A report that lists the profits of a pro: A report listing profits and owners is a financial statement, not a review of what happened and how to improve.
ww.A party held after a project ends to tha: A party thanking the team is a celebration or morale event and not a structured review of what happened and why.

rw: Onboarding helps new employees quickly learn what the organization knows, such as processes, culture and tools, so they become productive sooner.

ww.Removing information from the files so n: Removing information from files so new hires cannot see it blocks learning, the opposite of onboarding, which shares organizational knowledge.
ww.Preventing new hires from asking questio: Onboarding encourages new hires to ask questions, so preventing questions would slow learning and defeat the purpose of onboarding.
ww.Delaying training until employees ask fo: Delaying training until employees request it in writing slows learning, while good onboarding gives knowledge early without waiting.

rw: Fear that sharing will reduce their value makes employees hold knowledge back, which is a common barrier to knowledge sharing.

ww.Clear tools that make documents easy to: Clear tools that make documents easy to find help sharing, so they are an enabler and not a barrier.
ww.Time set aside for teams to teach each o: Time set aside for teams to teach each other encourages sharing, so it supports knowledge sharing and is not a barrier.
ww.Rewards for helping coworkers learn new: Rewards for helping coworkers learn motivate sharing, so they help knowledge flow and are not a barrier.

rw: A wiki is a shared site that staff can edit together, building a common pool of knowledge that keeps improving over time.

ww.A locked file that only one person can r: A locked file that only one person can read or change is the opposite of a wiki, which is open for collaboration.
ww.A calendar for scheduling holidays and s: A calendar for scheduling holidays is a planning tool and not a place where staff build and edit shared knowledge.
ww.A tool for printing business cards for t: Printing business cards is a printing task, while a wiki is an online tool for collecting and sharing knowledge.

rw: Data security means protecting data from unauthorized access, loss or damage, using tools such as passwords, encryption and backups.

ww.Posting the data online so that everyone: Posting data online for everyone would expose it to misuse, so it is the opposite of data security.
ww.Sharing passwords among all employees in: Sharing passwords among all employees weakens security because anyone could access data and actions could not be traced to individuals.
ww.Deleting all data after it has been used: Deleting data after one use would destroy information the business may need, and it is not a data security practice.

rw: Strong passwords and encryption keep company data safe even if a laptop is lost or stolen, since unauthorized people cannot read it.

ww.Using the same password on every account: Using the same password on every account is risky, because one breach would expose all of the accounts at once.
ww.Writing passwords on sticky notes: Writing passwords on sticky notes lets anyone who sees them steal access, which makes it an insecure habit.
ww.Leaving laptops unlocked in public place: Leaving unlocked laptops in public places invites theft and unauthorized access to company data, so it is poor practice.

rw: Backups keep copies of important files so they can be restored if the original is lost, damaged or deleted, protecting the business from data loss.

ww.So the files can never be changed again: Backups do not prevent file changes; their purpose is recovery, and users can still edit the original files.
ww.So no one else can open the files at any: Backups are meant to help restore access, and they do not stop others from opening files in the future.
ww.So the files take up more space and slow: Backups use extra storage, but that is a cost and not their purpose, and they should not slow the computer.

rw: A standard operating procedure is a written set of steps for doing a task the same way each time, which improves consistency, quality and training.

ww.A list of the products a firm sells to i: A list of products a firm sells is a catalog and not a set of steps for doing a task consistently.
ww.A report on a firm's quarterly results f: A report on quarterly results for investors is a financial report and not a step-by-step work procedure.
ww.A schedule of when employees take breaks: A break schedule sets time off and is a staffing document, not a written procedure for doing a task.

rw: Step-by-step written instructions for a routine task are a standard operating procedure, which keeps work consistent from day to day.

ww.A lease agreement for the building: A lease agreement is a legal contract for renting the building and does not give steps for opening the restaurant.
ww.A financial report for investors: A financial report for investors shows money results and does not describe steps for opening the restaurant each morning.
ww.A marketing plan for new customers: A marketing plan outlines how to attract customers and does not give steps for opening the restaurant.

rw: Quality is how well a product or service meets customer needs and expectations, including reliability, performance and satisfaction.

ww.How many products a company sells in a g: How many products a company sells is sales volume, which does not tell whether those products meet customer needs.
ww.How large a product is when it is packag: The packaged size of a product is a physical attribute, and size alone does not define quality.
ww.How expensive a product is to produce in: Production cost describes expense to the firm, and it does not show how well a product meets customer needs.

rw: Quality assurance is planned activities that prevent defects from happening, such as training, standards and process design, built into production from the start.

ww.Reducing the number of inspections to sa: Reducing inspections to save money may let defects through; quality assurance is planned prevention, not cutting checks to save cost.
ww.Paying customers to ignore defects in wh: Paying customers to ignore defects hides problems instead of fixing them, so it is not quality assurance.
ww.Checking finished products for defects o: Checking only finished products for defects is quality control, which detects problems after production rather than preventing them.

rw: Training workers on correct assembly steps before production prevents defects in advance, which is quality assurance because it focuses on the process.

ww.Inspecting finished items at the end and: Inspecting finished items and removing broken ones detects defects after the work is done, which is quality control and not assurance.
ww.Counting the number of items rejected la: Counting the items rejected last week measures results after the fact, which is a quality control measure and not prevention.
ww.Testing a sample of items after they are: Testing a sample of items after packing finds defects after production, so it is quality control rather than quality assurance.

rw: A defect is a flaw that makes a product fail to meet standards or customer expectations, such as a crack or wrong size.

ww.A package that is colorful and attractiv: A colorful package is an appearance feature and not a flaw that makes a product fail its standards.
ww.A price that is lower than rivals' price: A price lower than rivals is a pricing advantage and does not mean the product fails to meet quality standards.
ww.A feature that customers love and often: A feature customers love is a strength and not a flaw, so it cannot be a defect.

rw: Total quality management is a company-wide approach in which every employee works for continuous improvement and customer satisfaction.

ww.A method that focuses only on lowering p: TQM is not only about lowering prices; it focuses on quality and customer satisfaction, not on price cutting alone.
ww.A method that ignores customer feedback: TQM uses customer feedback and complaints as inputs for improvement, so ignoring them is the opposite of the method.
ww.A method where only inspectors are respo: In TQM everyone shares responsibility for quality, so it is not left only to inspectors.

rw: Continuous improvement means making ongoing small changes that raise quality and efficiency over time, as in the Japanese practice of Kaizen.

ww.Waiting for customers to complain before: Waiting for complaints is reactive; continuous improvement looks for ways to get better without waiting for customers to report problems.
ww.Avoiding any change to existing methods: Avoiding change to methods stops improvement, which is the opposite of the continuous effort to get better.
ww.Making one large change and never changi: Making one large change and never changing again is a one-time fix, while continuous improvement is a steady, repeated effort.

rw: Weekly meetings finding small ways to cut waste show continuous improvement, in which teams keep making small gains in quality and efficiency.

ww.Price fixing by rivals: Price fixing by rivals is an illegal agreement on prices, and it has nothing to do with a team reducing waste.
ww.Channel conflict in retail: Channel conflict arises when distribution partners compete, which has no relation to a factory team reducing waste.
ww.Market skimming plans: Market skimming plans, or price skimming, set a high initial price on a new product, which is unrelated to cutting waste in production.
